issue_context.title: OSSL_sleep() on unix maps to usleep(3) which does not handle large values
issue_context.body:
I ran into this by looking at why test/sanitytest fails for me.
Turns out the test tries to sleep for 1 second calling OSSL_sleep(1000).

But the unix implementation of OSSL_sleep() in most parts of the #ifdef cascade maps to `usleep(millis1000).

This has two problems:

  - usleep() has been removed from Posix, applications are recommended to use nanosleep() instead
  - usleep() does not work for times >= 1 second at least on some systems, see e.g. [usleep(3)](https://man.netbsd.org/usleep.3)
comments: Suggest we consider using OSSL_TIME and a custom sleep function.

We should probably loop if millis >= 1000, so that we do multiple invocations of the sleep functions which are all less than 1 second.

> Suggest we consider using OSSL_TIME and a custom sleep function.

Converting it to use OSSL_TIME internally wouldn't be a bad idea for master - but I guess the "custom sleep function" is still the same sleep code that we are currently using - but converted to use OSSL_TIME instead.

I'd call this a bug if this is causing tests to fail on real systems.

The conversion to use nanosleep instead probably is more of a feature. At least until we encounter real systems that don't have usleep. We'd somehow need to detect the existence of nanosleep()  (perhaps by checking the claimed POSIX support level??).

Looping is not a good idea unless it cannot be avoided. We could convert this to call usleep() for the < 1 second plus sleep() for the whole seconds portion. It is still less than ideal as every sleep/usleep call yields CPU to other processes but definitely better than calling usleep() in a loop.

review_comments:
What happens on a system where `unsigned int` is 32 bits, but the value of `millis` is greater than 2^42 (approx)?

While it's clearly an edge case, someone might be pretty much expecting "sleep for ever" and get "return almost immediately"
We did not check the overflow before with the usleep() call and do not for above usleep() calls either.
Yes, but we do in the `_WIN32` case below - wouldn't this be a better pattern for all of the sleep implementations?
Err, not sure I've been clear: I would prefer if we did do checking, as is done in the `_WIN32` case. Sorry, but I'm not sure if your comment means you agree or disagree!
I agree. Whether it needs to be done in this PR or whether it can be a separate one, that's another question. This one is already approved.
